normalized_proposition: The Regulation governs differentiated objects: AI systems, general-purpose AI models, high-risk systems, certain prohibited practices, and specified risks and interests.
The Regulation identifies covered operator and affected-person categories and limits its personal and material scope.
Providers of high-risk AI systems must meet risk-management, data-governance, documentation, logging, transparency/oversight-design, quality-management and post-market-monitoring duties.
Deployers have separate use and human-oversight obligations for high-risk systems.
Third-party conformity assessment is part of defined routes; Art. 43 does not make notified-body involvement universal.
Provider cooperation and reporting duties connect to Member State market surveillance; the Union safeguard procedure applies to national measures.
Designated fundamental-rights authorities may access specified documentation and must inform the market surveillance authority.

Chapter V assigns exclusive supervision/enforcement of general-purpose AI model obligations to the Commission, implemented by the AI Office, with alert, information, evaluation and measure provisions.
Member States designate notifying authorities to assess, designate, notify and monitor conformity-assessment bodies.
Public authority is allocated by function across Member State and Union actors, including a distinct Commission Chapter V remit.
Legal discretion is bounded and function-specific (conformity-route choice, deployer resource organisation, corrective decisions).
Information duties support oversight; hearing, judicial review and procedural safeguards before fines provide more structured answerability features.
Additional statement-level evidence propositions in provisions not individually anchored in V8's claims (e.g. Arts. 4, 8, 27, 35–42, 44–50, 56–71, 78, 85–87, 95–98, 102–113 and Annexes).
The provider accompanies the high-risk system with instructions for use and human-oversight information for the deployer; the deployer uses the system in accordance with instructions.
The provider may choose a notified body for the conformity assessment route; the notified body verifies conformity of the provider's system under the applicable procedure.

The notifying authority assesses applications of conformity-assessment bodies, designates, notifies and monitors them; the body applies and updates its documentation; Member States may assign assessment to the national accreditation body.

The Commission and other Member States may object to a notification of a conformity-assessment body within two weeks or two months; the body may act as notified body only if no objection is raised; the Commission enters into consultations on objections.

On a reasoned request by a competent authority the provider supplies information, documentation and logs demonstrating conformity: whether the receiving party is a 'national competent authority' (notifying authority or market surveillance authority, Art. 3(48)) or the broader 'competent authority' used in Art. 21.
The provider reports serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State where the incident occurred; the provider cooperates in investigations.

Post-market and incident information chain: deployers inform providers/distributors and authorities; authorities inform fundamental-rights bodies and the Commission (Art. 73(7), (11)); providers may receive deployer data.
The market surveillance authority evaluates an AI system presenting a risk or non-compliance, requires corrective action and takes provisional measures; operators cooperate.

The authority notifies the Commission of a provisional measure; the Commission consults, evaluates and decides within six months (60 days for Art. 5 prohibitions) whether the national measure is justified; where justified, all Member States must take appropriate restrictive measures and inform the Commission.

Designated fundamental-rights authorities may request and access documentation within their mandate and inform the market surveillance authority; the market surveillance authority organises testing with them.

The Commission (AI Office) supervises providers of general-purpose AI models: requests documentation and information, evaluates, requests measures, may make commitments binding, fines, with provider duties to supply information and access.
The scientific panel may issue qualified alerts and substantiated requests and may be appointed by the Commission to evaluate; the panel is established by a Commission implementing act (Art. 68(1)).
The Commission informs and consults the Board before exercising Chapter V powers and evaluations and communicates information on fines.

Operator value chain: importers and distributors verify conformity assessment, CE marking and declaration and inform providers/authorities; distributors ensure corrective action; providers appoint authorised representatives; a distributor, importer, deployer or third party is treated as provider in stated circumstances (Art. 25).
Deployers assign human oversight to competent natural persons and cooperate with competent authorities.

Relations toward natural persons: information on exposure and use (Art. 26(7), (11), Art. 50), consent and withdrawal in real-world testing (Art. 61), right to explanation (Art. 86), complaints taken into account by market surveillance authorities (Art. 85).

Law-enforcement real-time and post-remote biometric identification: authorisation by a judicial or independent administrative authority, notification of each use to the market surveillance and data-protection authorities, annual reporting to the Commission and publication, applicable where a Member State provides for authorisation by national law.

Codes of practice and conduct: the AI Office and Board facilitate and monitor codes of practice for general-purpose AI models; providers adhere and report; the Commission may approve a code by implementing act; voluntary codes of conduct are facilitated.

Standardisation requests, common specifications and presumptions of conformity: the Commission requests harmonised standards, may adopt common specifications where standards are not delivered or insufficient, consults the Board and advisory forum; conformity with standards or specifications gives a presumption.

Sandboxes and real-world testing: Member States establish sandboxes; participation follows a plan agreed with the competent authority; real-world testing requires market surveillance approval and may be suspended or terminated; exit reports are taken into account by authorities and notified bodies; reports go to the AI Office and Board.
Registration and access around the EU database: providers and deployers register; the Commission is controller; market surveillance authorities access and check.

Union governance bodies: the Board and advisory forum advise the Commission and Member States; the Commission provides the secretariat and consults them; the scientific panel supports market surveillance authorities.

Delegation of power: Parliament and Council confer the power to adopt delegated acts (five years, tacitly renewable), may revoke it and may object; the Commission reports, notifies and consults Member State experts.
The Commission is assisted by a committee under the examination procedure when adopting implementing acts (Art. 98(2)); the Commission informs the committee in stated cases.

Fines: Member States set penalty rules and notify them; fines on operators and notified bodies are imposed by the competent authority or court (Art. 99(9)); the EDPS fines Union bodies; the Commission fines general-purpose-model providers; the Court of Justice reviews Commission fines with unlimited jurisdiction.
The EDPS acts as competent authority, market surveillance authority and fining authority for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies and participates in the Board as observer.
Member States establish or designate authorities, ensure their resources and notify the Commission of authorities, rules and fines (Art. 28, 57(1), 70, 77(2), 99(2)).
For high-risk systems used by law-enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or Union bodies, the market surveillance authority acts as notified body in the Annex VII procedure.

Where an AI system is based on a general-purpose AI model by the same provider, the AI Office has the powers of a market surveillance authority; market surveillance authorities cooperate with the AI Office, inform the Board and may request enforcement of access to model information; they may request the Commission to exercise Chapter V powers.

High-risk lifecycle and conformity: provider/deployer duties, conditional third-party assessment and (where included) operator-chain verification, designation of notified bodies and standards form one arrangement.
Designation of notified bodies (notifying authority, Commission objection, supervision, restriction) belongs with market surveillance (V8) or with the conformity-assessment arrangement (RGAM).

National market surveillance with Union safeguard: authority evaluation and measures, Commission review, operator cooperation duties, incident reporting and fundamental-rights access form one arrangement, versus separate arrangements for evaluation/measures (with Union review), operator duties toward authorities, and post-market/incident reporting.
Commission-centred supervision and enforcement of general-purpose AI models with AI Office implementation, panel alerts, Board consultation and provider-facing measures.

Rule-making arrangements: delegation of power with parliamentary/Council oversight (Art. 97) and implementing-act competences under the committee procedure (Art. 98) form arrangements of Commission secondary rule-making.
Codes of practice/conduct, and standardisation requests, common specifications and presumptions of conformity, form compliance-route arrangements.
Sandboxes and real-world testing form an authority-gated arrangement.
Union governance bodies (Board, advisory forum, scientific panel, AI Office, Member State representatives) form an arrangement of consultation, advice and secretariat relations.
Registration and access around the EU database form an arrangement controlled by the Commission.
Relations toward natural persons (information, explanation, consent, complaint) form an arrangement.
Authorisation, notification and reporting for law-enforcement biometric identification form an arrangement that operates only where Member States provide for authorisation by national law.
Penalties and fines (Member State, EDPS, Commission, Court of Justice review) and EDPS supervision of Union bodies form arrangements.
Establishment and notification of national authorities and Member State resources form an arrangement.

Overlap and integration among arrangements: V8's K01 and K02 share relations (R04, R05) and K03 is stated not to be collapsed into national surveillance; RGAM records explicit overlaps and source-supported couplings (Art. 43(1) third subparagraph, Art. 57(7), Art. 75, Art. 79(2), Art. 83, the EU database, Board consultations).
Differentiation: distinct governance pathways for high-risk systems and for general-purpose AI models.
Multilevel distribution: legally linked national and Union roles in the market-surveillance pathway.
The architecture is 'hybrid': it combines operator-internal duties, external conformity assessment in defined routes, and public authority.

Number and boundary of architectures: one differentiated, hybrid, multilevel architecture of the whole Regulation (K01–K03), versus nine architecture candidates (five INTEGRATED provisional, one OVERLAPPING_OR_PARTIALLY_INTEGRATED, three INDETERMINATE) with the whole instrument partially integrated and no whole-level property attributable.
National enforcement path: operator reports or authority findings at national level can end in a Commission decision binding all Member States, with operators bound to supply documentation.
Union-level path for general-purpose models: classification, obligations, requests, evaluations, measures and fines with the same authority at each step and judicial review.

RGAM architecture candidates for the delegation of power (INTEGRATED provisional) and for sandboxes (INTEGRATED provisional), and an INDETERMINATE rule-making candidate (delegated and implementing acts); no V8 counterpart.
RGAM architecture candidates not accepted at architecture level (INDETERMINATE): Union coordination bodies (ARCH-07) and biometric-identification control (ARCH-08).
Conformity architecture: two-route conformity path whose outputs are verified downstream and whose certifiers are designated and supervised with Union objection and review.

Accountability as a property: information duties are not by themselves accountability (both); where accountability features are located: hearing, judicial review and procedural safeguards before fines (V8) versus provider duties to supply information and access combined with questioning, assessment and consequences, classed ACCOUNTABILITY (derived) with sufficiency indeterminate, and answerability-only for duties to demonstrate conformity (RGAM).

Necessity/alternative-path claims: whether notified-body involvement is necessary for Annex I Section A systems and for Annex III systems, and whether the Art. 79–83 procedure has an alternative path (Art. 74(4)), given sectoral legislation outside the Regulation.
common_corpus_refs: Art. 43(1)–(3); Art. 74(4); Art. 79–83; Annex I Section A

normalized_proposition: Exclusive Commission competence over Chapter V and no national supervisory competence over it other than cooperation and requests.
No general power to instruct national market surveillance authorities, apart from Commission decisions under Arts. 46(5) and 81 and Art. 75 powers.
Decision-centre plurality in market surveillance: at least one authority per Member State and the Commission; the number is not stated.
Public/private character of notified bodies: established under national law with legal personality, independent of providers; whether public or private is not stated.
Bounded autonomy: operator-internal control within the high-risk lifecycle (V8) versus bounded provider autonomy in codes of practice approved and monitored by the Commission (RGAM).
Depth from the rule-making position is not attributable: delegated acts amend objects, not relations.

Discretion distribution: V8 records bounded function-specific discretion for provider route choice, deployer organisation and authority measures; RGAM records authority discretion over corrective periods and provisional measures and Commission decision within periods.
The claims concern formal legal design; implementation, compliance, effectiveness and prevalence are not asserted.

External legal dependencies as sensitivity of conclusions: the content of market-surveillance powers (Reg. 2019/1020), Annex I Section A legislation, the examination procedure (Reg. 182/2011), the AI Office as a Commission function, the implementing act establishing the scientific panel, accessibility, financial-services and copyright law; claims about them should or should not be limited to the Regulation's text.

Application dates and legal status: the Regulation applies from 2 August 2026 with staged dates (Chapters I–II from 2 February 2025; Chapter V and others from 2 August 2025 except Art. 101; Art. 6(1) from 2 August 2027); RGAM states the status at the reference point 2 August 2026 and records 15 relations as conditional on further acts; V8 states no reference date.

Rival groupings and boundary sensitivities for architecture(s): treating overlaps as couplings gives partial integration, treating them as incidental gives distinguishable candidates; Art. 75 as coupling or not; separate sandboxes and real-world testing; separate delegation and implementing acts.

Stopping level: both stop at the architectural level (no regime claim); RGAM stops below the architectural level for three candidates (INDETERMINATE) and for the whole instrument (partial integration), where V8 asserts one architecture.

Confidence in the architecture claim: V8 states 'High' confidence for the whole-level claim and its configurations while recording moderate confidence for significance versus prevalence (U07); RGAM states provisional outcomes with unvalidated coupling thresholds and indeterminate outcomes for three candidates.
Higher-order constructs: governance logic, strategy, regime membership beyond the architecture.
Information duties alone are not accountability; accountability sufficiency is uncertain where no forum, assessment capacity or consequence is stated.

Direction/counterparty uncertainty where the text names no party (e.g. who provides the system to the deployer, Art. 14(4); addressee of objections, Art. 30; of complaints, Art. 89(2); requester under Art. 5(3)).
Source ambiguities in wording (undefined terms such as 'affected persons', compound permissions, ambiguous constitution of the advisory forum and notified bodies).
Norm-type taxonomy (N0–N4, compound or ambiguous) of drafting forms such as 'may ... provided that all conditions are met'.
